extracted.intended_audience: Readers of The Spectator; early-18th-century English polite society (gentlemen and ladies)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance (essays) on personal conduct: sincerity, decorum, dress, pedantry, treatment of servants, and the qualities desirable in clergy and masters, as presented in The Spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and Plainness over Compliment and Dissimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity and Plainness (the old English plainness and sincerity, generous integrity of nature) are preferable to a conversation swelled with vanity and compliment; our language is running into a lie when words signify nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliment is hollow — 'Words are like Money' but often mere cyphers; dissembling brings perpetual inconvenience because it 'brings a Man under an everlasting Jealousie and Suspicion, so that he is not believed when he speaks Truth, nor trusted when perhaps he means honestly.' Prefer being genuinely what you would seem to be; dissimulation is ultimately self-defeating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not counterfeit qualities; be what you would seem to be
rubrics_metrics.description: To counterfeit and dissemble is to put on the appearance of some real excellency; the best way to seem to be anything is really to be what you would seem to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretence is often more troublesome than possession of the quality; a man who lacks a quality is likely to be discovered and then loses all the pains spent to seem to have it. Practical rule: cultivate the real quality rather than the appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adopting foreign fashions that corrupt native manners
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been a long endeavour to transform us into foreign manners and fashions, bringing a servile imitation of neighbours (often importing vanity and compliment into our dialect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitating foreign modes can erode 'English' plainness and sincerity. Be cautious of novel fashions and affected phrases that circulate as current payment but carry low intrinsic value; favour native simplicity and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency (Decorum) as a rule of life linked to virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorum or a regard to decency in dress, words, and actions is nearly related to virtue; decency of behaviour obtains approbation through order, consistency, and moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behave with moderation and attention to how words and actions fit together; neglecting what others think shows arrogance. For women, a useful rule: in dress, words, and actions recommend yourself as a sister, daughter, or wife. Decency commands respect because it shows deference to others' good opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clear gender-appropriate distinctions in dress and carriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing male and female dress (e.g., Amazonian hunting-habit with petticoat or women assuming male airs) confuses propriety and breaks the distinction preserving beauty of different characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women should 'be themselves' as Nature designed; avoid adopting men's dress or effeminate airs. Such mixtures create perplexities and may turn public assemblies into a masquerade; preserve the proper character signalled by attire and carriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of dissimulation: loss of credibility is lasting
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man has once forfeited the reputation of his integrity, he is set fast, and nothing will then serve his turn, neither truth nor falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissimulation breeds everlasting suspicion: the dishonest speaker will not be believed even when truthful; thus honesty preserves future credibility and social capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry and narrowness of conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: A pedant is anyone brought up among books (or a 'mere' courtier, soldier, scholar, etc.) who cannot think or converse beyond his profession or narrow sphere; such people are insipid and ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden the circle of observation beyond one's immediate sphere (town, court, camp, Westminster-Hall, the Gazette). The essay catalogs varieties of pedants (man of the town, military pedant, law-pedant, state-pedant, book-pedant) as anti-patterns to social adaptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning without common sense makes a person insufferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning, like travelling, finishes good sense; but learning alone, without taste or distinction, makes a silly man ten thousand times more insufferable by supplying matter to his impertinence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate judgement and taste alongside learning; be wary of those who have read much yet lack common sense — they tend to be vain, arrogant, and prone to absurdities (e.g., lavishing exaggerated praise over trivial scholarly acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicion of mutual, lavish scholarly praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Shallow pedants cry up one another; to read the titles they give an editor you might take him for the glory of letters when he has only made trivial corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of excessive praise among scholars; genuine merit requires distinguishing substance from superficial editorial or pedantic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parish clergyman virtues: plain sense, good aspect, clear voice, sociable temper
rubrics_metrics.description: For a country clergyman, 'plain Sense' and a good aspect, a clear voice, and a sociable temper are virtues to prefer, even over ostentatious learning; a graceful delivery of established good sermons is highly edifying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than labouring in ambitious compositions, clergy should cultivate elocution and delivery to enforce what greater masters have penned; a well-delivered sermon (like a poet's composition in the mouth of a graceful actor) is more edifying than abstruse learning unreadable to the congregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good masters treat servants humanely and create respect
rubrics_metrics.description: The general corruption of servants' manners often results from masters' conduct; a master who governs with benevolence and economy obtains respect and cheerful performance of duty — orders are received as favours rather than burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid harshness and petty punishments; show interest in servants' welfare, employ them with respect, and reward them in ways that produce loyalty and diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward servants by enabling independent livelihoods, not trinkets
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving cast clothes or trifling gifts creates a silly sense of equality; a true reward is putting a good servant in a way of livelihood (apprenticeship, settlement) or forgiving large fines — making them independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer substantial rewards (land, annuity, settlement, apprenticeship) that improve a servant's life and encourage successors to be diligent, rather than merely bestowing diminutive tokens that may humiliate or create false parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household order and continuity reflect good management
rubrics_metrics.description: Long service, stable domestics, and uniform civility in the family show good management; the appearance of contented aged servants and consistent behaviour is evidence of a good master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent treatment of household staff, keep servants long when deserved, and demonstrate kindness publicly (which elicits genuine affection and loyalty rather than fear).
